content_voiceover: This is the completed protein C anticoagulation pathway. Activated protein C, now paired with its cofactor protein S, shown as the green S, forms a complex on the membrane surface. This APC-protein S complex is the business end of the pathway: it proteolytically cleaves factor Va, converting it into an inactivated form labeled Vi, and separately cleaves factor VIIIa into inactivated VIIIa, shown crossed out. Because Va and VIIIa are essential cofactors for the prothrombinase and intrinsic tenase complexes, destroying them shuts down thrombin generation at two points simultaneously. This is exactly why factor V Leiden is clinically important: that mutation makes factor Va resistant to cleavage by activated protein C, producing a hypercoagulable state called APC resistance, one of the most common inherited thrombophilias tested on boards.
keypoints: APC plus protein S degrade factor Va and VIIIa
Loss of Va and VIIIa halts thrombin generation
Factor V Leiden causes APC resistance
APC resistance is the most common inherited thrombophilia
keypoint_voiceover: Activated protein C together with protein S inactivates factors Va and VIIIa, cutting off both the prothrombinase and intrinsic tenase complexes at once. Factor V Leiden resists this cleavage, producing a state called APC resistance, which is the single most common inherited thrombophilia tested on hematology boards.
